nodes.claim: For t=1,...,T, output x_t in V subset R^d, pay loss ell_t(x_t) for ell_t:V->R, then receive some feedback on ell_t.
nodes.sourceText: Output x_t ∈ V ⊆ R^d; Pay the loss ℓ_t(x_t), where ℓ_t : V → R; Receive some feedback on ℓ_t.
nodes.scope: Round-index, feasible action, real losses on V, and output-before-loss/feedback convention. T is a finite horizon; no special threshold. This is a standing game definition, not a new FTL theorem.

nodes.claim: Regret_T(u) = sum_{t=1}^T ell_t(x_t) - sum_{t=1}^T ell_t(u), for any fixed competitor u in V.
nodes.scope: Context only. No rate, expectation, confidence event or regret guarantee is part of this FTL definition anchor.

nodes.claim: The chapter focuses for a while on convex losses, called Online Convex Optimization; the p11 lead-in specializes the coming algorithm discussion to convex differentiable functions.
nodes.scope: Context for this presentation. Convexity/differentiability do not by themselves guarantee cumulative-loss attainment or unique FTL choices. No closedness/compactness imported from OGD.

nodes.claim: V subset R^d is convex when lambda*x+(1-lambda)*y belongs to V for x,y in V and lambda in (0,1).
nodes.scope: Terminology only, not a new FTL-specific hypothesis. The empty set satisfies this condition vacuously; playable initialization still requires a feasible point.

nodes.claim: For an extended-real-valued function on R^d, dom f = {x in R^d : f(x)<+infinity}.
nodes.scope: The chapter allows extended-real notation; the online game itself states real losses on V. This source definition does not exclude -infinity in dom f. No global unrestricted extended-real FTL arithmetic is asserted.

compressedExplanation: FTL chooses a feasible action minimizing cumulative loss from strictly earlier rounds 1 through t-1. The first round has no past losses, so the source permits any feasible action. The source leaves existence of later minimizers and tie-selection/access mechanics unspecified. This is an algorithmic prescription with conditional applicability, not a rate theorem.
